scenes.heading: fake_api.py: a script, not a model
scenes.title: productivity/fake_api.py

steps.note: It can't understand free-form requests: always phrase demos simply.

tokens: """An offline stand-in for the Anthropic Messages API.
It speaks the same HTTP protocol as the real API, so the real `anthropic`
SDK and the agent loop run unchanged. Instead of a model it follows a fixed
script: it splits the request on "and" or ";", matches each part against a
few simple patterns ("add task ...", "list tasks", "delete task 2"), asks for
ALL the matching tool calls in one turn (parallel tool use), then writes a
placeholder answer that lists the tool results. That is NOT model output: it
can't understand free-form requests, plan, or recover on its own. Use it for
tests, demos and learning without an API key.

scenes.title: Saving safely: write the new page, then swap
scenes.body: Editing a document by hand, you could tear out a page and then get interrupted before writing the new one. Safer: **write the new page first, then swap** it in. That's an atomic save: you always have the old file or the new file, **never half of one**.

captions.text: Project time.
Over two lessons we'll build a personal productivity agent: you tell it, in plain
words, what to do with your tasks and notes, and it uses six tools to do it, safely.
Everything from this module comes together here.
We'll go one file at a time.
Here's what we're building.
You ask in plain words, at the command line, like: add task pay rent, and list
tasks.
The agent has six tools, for tasks and notes, defined once in a registry, with
schemas from Pydantic.
Every input is validated, and every tool has a timeout.
Tools have permission levels, there's a read-only mode, and deleting needs a human
yes.
And the data is saved safely in a JSON file, with forty-three tests and an offline
mode.
Here's the plan.
The command line passes your request to the agent, which runs the loop from Module
Every tool call goes through tools dot py: the registry, validation, and timeouts.
It asks the policy for permission, and the tools read and write the store.
And the agent talks to the model through the client: the real Claude API with a key,
or the offline fake without one.
First, so you know exactly what you're seeing in this video: the offline fake.
It speaks the same protocol as the real API, so the SDK and the loop run unchanged.
It splits your request on the word and, matches each part against a few patterns,
and asks for all the matching tools in one turn.
That's not a model.
It can't understand free-form requests, so the demos use simple phrases.
No API key was used in this recording.
The tools, the validation, the timeouts, and the policy are all completely real.
Now the store, where tasks and notes live.
Imagine editing a notebook.
If you tear out a page, and then get interrupted before writing the new one, the
page is just gone.
The safe way is to write the new page first, and then swap it in.
That's called an atomic save.
At any moment, you have either the old file or the new file, never half of one.
Load reads the JSON file.
If there's no file yet, we start with empty lists of tasks and notes.
Save writes everything to a temporary file, then os dot replace swaps it in, in one
step.
If the program crashes halfway through writing, the real file is untouched.
New items get the next ID: one more than the biggest ID so far.
And every change follows the same three steps: load, modify, save.
Add task creates a task with the next ID, appends it, and saves.
Let's look at the tools.
List tasks is a read tool.
Its description tells the model to use it before completing or deleting, to find the
task's number.
Complete task is a write tool.
It needs the number from list tasks.
Delete task is danger.
Its description warns the model to use it only when the user clearly asks, and to
prefer complete task for finishing.
And it has a confirm function, which builds the question the human sees.
Add note is a write tool, that saves an idea or meeting notes.
And search notes is read, with a shorter, two-second timeout, because in a real app
it would call a remote search service.
Here's how the command line wires it together.
Ask human prints the question, with y slash capital N, so no is the default, and
reads one line.
Piped input works too, which is how the demos answer.
For each request, we build the context, and the policy.
The read-only flag sets read-only mode.
And the yes flag approves dangerous actions automatically, which is useful for
scripts you trust, and dangerous anywhere else.
Then the agent gets the client, the cost tracker, the context, and the policy, and
runs the request, printing each step as it happens.
Finally, a footer with turns, tool calls and cost, and the answer.
Any ending other than answered becomes one clear error, exactly like Module 4.
Let's run it.
The tools command shows every tool, with its permission and timeout.
Reset gives us an empty store.
It deletes data, so it asks first too, unless we pass yes.
And a first request with three parts.
Look at the trace: three tool calls, all in turn one.
That's a parallel tool call.
Two tasks and a note, saved, in two turns in total.
Pause and predict.
The store has tasks one and two.
The request is: complete task two, and delete task seven.
The human would say yes if asked.
How many tool calls are there?
Is the human asked?
And what does each call return?
Two tool calls, both in turn one.
Complete task two succeeds.
Delete task seven fails before anyone is asked, with: there is no task seven.
The human is never asked about a task that doesn't exist.
